questions.stem: An 8 year old boy develops an itchy rash 30 minutes after his second dose of amoxicillin for tonsillitis. He has raised, pale-centred red wheals on his trunk and limbs that move around over a few hours. He has no lip swelling, wheeze or dizziness. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 96 bpm, BP 104/66 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Itchy, transient wheals soon after a drug trigger without ABC compromise is acute urticaria, an IgE-mediated allergic reaction. Anaphylaxis needs airway, breathing or circulation involvement.

clues: 30 minutes after his second dose of amoxicillin
no lip swelling, wheeze or dizziness
steps.x: Itchy wheals shortly after a trigger, with normal observations.

elim: No airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
Target lesions that are fixed for days, not migrating wheals.
Maculopapular rash with cough, conjunctivitis and coryza, spreading from behind the ears.
Sandpaper-like rash with strawberry tongue, not itchy wheals.

steps.x: A: Acute urticaria. Wheals soon after a trigger, no ABC problem = acute urticaria.

questions.stem: A 25 year old man has had a blocked, runny nose and sneezing all year round for 2 years. Symptoms are worst on waking and when he makes his bed. His eyes are itchy and watery. He had eczema as a child. His temperature is 36.7°C. The nasal mucosa is pale and swollen with clear discharge and there are no polyps.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Year-round sneezing, rhinorrhoea and itchy watery eyes, worse with bedding (house dust mite), in an atopic person is perennial allergic rhinitis.

clues: He had eczema as a child
steps.x: Year-round symptoms, a bedding trigger and atopy.

elim: No polyps are seen and eye itching is not a feature.
Caused by prolonged decongestant spray use, which is not described.
Symptoms are year round, not limited to the pollen season.
Does not last 2 years.

steps.x: B: Perennial allergic rhinitis. Year-round rhinitis with a dust mite trigger in an atopic patient = perennial allergic rhinitis.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl stays overnight at a friend's house where there are two cats. Within an hour of arriving her eyes become red, itchy and watery and she starts sneezing with a clear runny nose. She has hay fever. Her temperature is 36.8°C and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Both conjunctivae are injected with no discharge other than tears. Visual acuity is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Itchy watery red eyes with sneezing and rhinorrhoea shortly after cat exposure in an atopic patient is allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.

steps.x: Rapid onset after an allergen in an atopic teenager, bilateral itch.

elim: Painful red eye with reduced vision and a fixed pupil.
Purulent sticky discharge, usually without sneezing.
Localised, sectoral redness without itch or rhinitis.
Follows a cold, with lymphadenopathy, not an hour after cat exposure.

steps.x: B: Allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. Itch, conjunctival redness and rhinorrhoea after exposure = allergic.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy has developed urticaria and vomiting within minutes of eating scrambled egg on two occasions. His mother asks why he has allergies when his friends do not. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 100 bpm. Examination shows dry, flexural skin. His total IgE has not been measured.
questions.q: Which is the strongest risk factor for his allergy?
o: Normal total IgE would exclude allergy
questions.e: Atopy (eczema, asthma, hay fever) is a major risk factor for IgE-mediated allergy, along with family history and previous reactions. IgE may be raised but is not required for diagnosis.

clues: within minutes of eating scrambled egg on two occasions
steps.x: Flexural dryness means atopic eczema.

elim: Not a recognised risk factor for allergy.
Not a major risk factor.
Total IgE may be raised but is not needed for diagnosis, and is not a risk factor.
Can cause urticaria but not repeated reactions to egg.

steps.x: D: Personal history of eczema. Atopy and family history are the key risk factors for allergy.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman develops swelling of her lips and around her eyes with itchy hives 15 minutes after eating a dessert containing hazelnuts. She takes no regular medication and has no family history of swelling. Her voice is normal and she has no stridor or wheeze. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lip and periorbital angioedema with urticaria minutes after a food trigger, without ABC compromise, is an IgE-mediated allergic reaction; it becomes anaphylaxis only with airway, breathing or circulation problems.

clues: 15 minutes after eating a dessert containing hazelnuts
steps.x: Angioedema with urticaria after food, normal observations.

elim: She takes no regular medication.
No airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
Unilateral, tender, hot swelling with fever, not minutes after food.
No family history and occurs without urticaria.

steps.x: B: Acute allergic reaction with angioedema. Angioedema plus hives after a trigger without ABC compromise = allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 6 week old girl is exclusively breastfed. For 3 weeks she has had loose stools with mucus and streaks of blood, frequent vomiting after feeds and worsening eczema. Her mother drinks a lot of milk. The baby is afebrile and alert, with a soft abdomen. Her weight has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Cow's milk protein allergy can occur even in exclusively breastfed infants through maternal dairy intake, presenting with multi-system symptoms (gut and skin) and faltering growth.

clues: Her mother drinks a lot of milk
steps.x: Gut and skin symptoms in a breastfed baby whose mother takes dairy.

elim: Crying without blood in the stool, eczema or weight loss.
Usually 6 to 18 months with colicky pain and redcurrant jelly stool.
Rare primary form in infants and does not cause eczema or bloody stools.
Projectile non-bilious vomiting without diarrhoea or eczema.

steps.x: A: Cow's milk protein allergy. Breastfed babies can have cow's milk protein allergy via maternal milk.

questions.stem: A 7 month old boy was diagnosed with non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy at 3 months, with reflux, loose stools and eczema. He improved on an extensively hydrolysed formula and is now thriving. His parents ask when he is likely to tolerate cow's milk. Examination is normal and his weight is on the 50th centile.
questions.q: By which age will he most likely tolerate cow's milk?
questions.e: Most children with non-IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy become tolerant by age 3, younger than with IgE-mediated allergy, which typically resolves before age 5.

clues: when he is likely to tolerate cow's milk
steps.x: Natural history of the non-IgE form.

elim: Far later than typical for either form.
Later than typical for non-IgE-mediated allergy.
Too early for most children; tolerance is tested with the milk ladder.
Most children outgrow cow's milk allergy.

steps.x: B: 3 years. Non-IgE cow's milk allergy: most tolerant by age 3.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 3 week history of itchy, red, scaly patches on her eyelids and cheeks. She started using a new face cream a month ago. The rash flares a day or two after each application and settles when she stops for a week. She has no lip swelling or breathing problems. Her temperature is 36.6°C. There is well-demarcated eczematous dermatitis where the cream is applied.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Eczematous dermatitis confined to the site of a cosmetic, appearing a day or two after contact, is allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed reaction diagnosed with patch testing.

clues: flares a day or two after each application
steps.x: Delayed dermatitis exactly where a cosmetic is applied.

elim: Transient wheals within minutes, not scaly patches days later.
Flushing, papules and pustules without a cream trigger.
Greasy scale on scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds, unrelated to a product.
Malar rash with systemic features, not linked to a cosmetic.

steps.x: B: Allergic contact dermatitis. Delayed eczematous rash at the contact site = allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.stem: A 15 year old girl with asthma and allergic rhinitis visits a friend with cats. Over 2 hours she becomes wheezy and short of breath, with sneezing and itchy eyes. She has no lip swelling, urticaria or dizziness. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. She has widespread expiratory wheeze and her peak flow is 55% of best.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her breathlessness?
questions.e: Allergen exposure can trigger an asthma exacerbation, a recognised complication of allergic disease; she has lower airway wheeze and a low peak flow without features of anaphylaxis.

steps.x: An atopic asthmatic exposed to her allergen, with wheeze and a low peak flow.

elim: No circulatory compromise, angioedema or urticaria; this is lower airway bronchospasm in an asthmatic.
No choking episode and the wheeze is widespread.
Wheeze is widespread and there is a clear allergic trigger.
Causes inspiratory noise, not widespread expiratory wheeze with a low peak flow.

steps.x: B: Exacerbation of asthma by allergen. Allergy complications include asthma exacerbation and anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has had itching of his mouth and lips, followed by hives on his neck, within 5 minutes of eating kiwi fruit on three occasions. Symptoms settle within an hour. He has hay fever. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 80 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Examination now is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Symptoms occurring within minutes of exposure (oral itch, urticaria) are IgE-mediated, driven by mast cell activation and histamine release.

clues: within 5 minutes of eating kiwi fruit
itching of his mouth and lips, followed by hives
steps.x: Rapid, reproducible oral itch and hives after one food.

elim: Non-immune, dose-related gut symptoms without hives.
Causes vomiting and diarrhoea hours later, not oral itch and hives within minutes.
Chronic bowel symptoms, not acute oral itch and urticaria.
Delayed onset over hours to days.

steps.x: C: IgE-mediated food allergy. Minutes after exposure with itch and hives = IgE-mediated.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with a known peanut allergy, previously causing only hives, eats a takeaway curry. Within 10 minutes his throat feels tight, his voice is hoarse and he feels faint. His pulse rate is 132 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% breathing air. He has widespread urticaria and inspiratory stridor.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis is the most serious complication of allergic disease: a sudden allergic reaction with airway, breathing and circulation compromise. A previous mild reaction does not predict a mild next one.

clues: known peanut allergy, previously causing only hives
steps.x: Airway and circulatory compromise after a known allergen.

elim: Does not cause stridor, hypoxia or hypotension.
Causes expiratory wheeze, not stridor with hypotension and urticaria.
Does not cause urticaria, stridor or hypotension.
Bradycardia, not tachycardia, stridor and urticaria.

steps.x: B: Anaphylaxis. Allergy with A, B or C compromise = anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman stung by a wasp in her garden 20 minutes ago has a red, swollen, itchy area on her forearm with a few wheals on her arm and chest. She has no lip swelling, voice change, wheeze or dizziness. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Itching, swelling and urticaria soon after a sting, without ABC compromise, is an IgE-mediated allergic reaction caused by histamine-driven vasodilation and increased permeability.

clues: stung by a wasp in her garden 20 minutes ago
a few wheals on her arm and chest
no lip swelling, voice change, wheeze or dizziness
steps.x: Local swelling plus distant wheals, normal observations.

elim: No airway, breathing or circulation compromise.
Develops over days with fever, not within 20 minutes.
A delayed reaction over days to a substance on the skin.
Requires multiple stings; she has itch and wheals of allergy.

steps.x: D: IgE-mediated allergic reaction with urticaria. Wheals soon after a trigger without ABC problems = allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has sneezing and itchy eyes each time she visits her brother's house, where there is a dog. Her GP refers her for skin prick testing to dog dander and other common allergens. She stopped her antihistamine a week ago. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. Examination is normal.
questions.q: Which substance is used as the positive control in this test?
questions.e: Skin prick testing places allergen drops on the forearm alongside a histamine positive control and a water or saline negative control; a fresh needle pricks each site and a wheal-and-flare shows IgE-mediated sensitisation.

clues: skin prick testing to dog dander
stopped her antihistamine a week ago
steps.x: Antihistamine stopped so the histamine control will work.

elim: Would cause vasoconstriction, not a wheal.
This is the negative control.
A local anaesthetic, not a control.
A blood marker of mast cell degranulation, not a skin test reagent.

steps.x: C: Histamine. Skin prick test: histamine positive control, water negative control.

questions.stem: A 2 year old boy has had lip swelling and hives twice within minutes of eating egg. He has severe eczema covering most of his arms, legs and back, and takes a daily antihistamine for itch that his parents do not want to stop. His temperature is 36.9°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. Examination shows widespread active eczema.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Specific IgE (RAST) measures allergen-specific IgE in blood and is a good indicator of food allergy; it is preferred when widespread eczema or antihistamines prevent skin prick testing.

clues: severe eczema covering most of his arms, legs and back
steps.x: Immediate food reaction, but skin testing is impractical.

elim: Will not confirm IgE sensitisation; the history is already clear.
Only confirms that an acute severe reaction has occurred.
Tests delayed contact allergy, not immediate food allergy.
Difficult with extensive eczema and daily antihistamines.

steps.x: E: Specific IgE (RAST) to egg. Skin prick not possible: use specific IgE (RAST).

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with asthma and eczema has a panel of specific IgE (RAST) tests. Results show raised IgE to peanut and to wheat. She has had urticaria after peanuts but eats bread and pasta every day with no symptoms. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. Examination shows mild flexural eczema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the wheat result?
o: False positive result due to atopy
True wheat allergy needing strict avoidance
questions.e: RAST can give false positives in atopic patients with eczema or asthma; results must be interpreted with the clinical history, and tolerated foods should not be avoided.

clues: eats bread and pasta every day with no symptoms
steps.x: An atopic patient with a positive test to a food she tolerates.

elim: Diagnosed with tTG antibodies, not specific IgE.
Less likely than the well-recognised false positives in atopic patients.
Would not raise specific IgE.
She tolerates wheat every day.

steps.x: B: False positive result due to atopy. Atopy causes false-positive RAST: interpret with the history.

questions.stem: A 40 year old man collapsed 10 minutes after a bee sting with wheeze and hypotension. He was given IM adrenaline by paramedics and has now recovered. Two hours have passed. His pulse rate is 90 bpm, BP 124/78 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. The allergy team will later want proof that a severe reaction occurred.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation now?
o: Skin prick testing to bee venom
questions.e: Mast cell tryptase rises after mast cell degranulation and confirms that an acute severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) has occurred.

clues: collapsed 10 minutes after a bee sting
proof that a severe reaction occurred
steps.x: Recent severe reaction, need biochemical confirmation.

elim: May be raised in atopy but does not confirm an acute reaction.
Tests delayed contact allergy.
Done later in allergy clinic, not acutely.
Shows sensitisation but not that anaphylaxis occurred.

steps.x: A: Mast cell tryptase. Confirm a severe allergic reaction with mast cell tryptase.

questions.stem: A 50 year old nurse has an itchy eczematous rash on both hands where her gloves touch. She is referred for skin patch testing with latex and other common contact allergens. The patches are applied to her back on Monday. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Examination shows dermatitis on both hands.
questions.q: When should the result most appropriately be read?
questions.e: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed T-cell-mediated reaction, so patch tests are assessed after 2 to 3 days.

clues: applied to her back on Monday
steps.x: A patch test for a delayed contact allergy.

elim: The timing for a skin prick test, which shows immediate IgE reactions.
Far too late.
Too early for a delayed T-cell reaction.
The delayed reaction has not developed yet.

steps.x: B: After 2 to 3 days. Patch testing: read at 2 to 3 days (Type IV).

questions.stem: A 4 month old formula-fed girl has had reflux, loose stools and eczema since starting formula at 6 weeks. Symptoms start hours to days after feeds. She is gaining weight along the 50th centile. Skin prick testing and specific IgE to cow's milk are negative. Her temperature is 36.8°C. Examination shows mild eczema.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic approach?
o: Trial cow's milk elimination for 2 to 6 weeks, then reintroduce
questions.e: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy is diagnosed clinically by elimination (2 to 6 weeks with a hypoallergenic formula) then reintroduction: improvement then recurrence confirms it.

clues: Skin prick testing and specific IgE to cow's milk are negative
steps.x: Delayed symptoms with negative IgE tests.

elim: Invasive and not needed for suspected milk allergy.
Tests lactose intolerance, not milk protein allergy.
Only confirms an acute severe reaction.
Non-IgE allergy gives negative skin prick tests.

steps.x: E: Trial cow's milk elimination for 2 to 6 weeks, then reintroduce. Non-IgE cow's milk allergy: eliminate 2 to 6 weeks, then reintroduce.

questions.stem: A 10 month old boy developed urticaria around his mouth and vomited within 10 minutes of his first taste of formula milk. He was breastfed until now and has mild eczema. He has no breathing difficulty. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. Examination now is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Cow's milk elimination and reintroduction at home
Skin prick testing to cow's milk
questions.e: Immediate symptoms after milk suggest IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy, confirmed by clinical history plus skin prick testing or specific IgE.

clues: within 10 minutes of his first taste of formula milk
steps.x: An immediate reaction after a first exposure to formula.

elim: Unsafe for an immediate IgE reaction; used for non-IgE allergy.
Tests lactose intolerance.
Tests delayed Type IV reactions.
No infective features.

steps.x: D: Skin prick testing to cow's milk. IgE-mediated cow's milk allergy: skin prick or specific IgE.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has had itchy wheals on his arms and trunk for 2 days after starting a new antibiotic, which has now been stopped. He has no lip swelling, wheeze or dizziness. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 82 bpm, BP 128/82 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. He drives for work.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Avoiding the trigger plus a non-sedating antihistamine such as cetirizine or loratadine is first-line treatment for allergic urticaria.

clues: itchy wheals on his arms and trunk
steps.x: Trigger removed, urticaria only, needs to stay alert.

elim: A sedating antihistamine; a non-sedating one is preferred, especially as he drives.
Only for anaphylaxis with ABC compromise.
Not first line for urticaria.
Steroids are added only if needed and never as a long course for this.

steps.x: C: Non-sedating antihistamine such as cetirizine. Allergic urticaria: avoid the trigger and give a non-sedating antihistamine.

questions.stem: A 29 year old teacher has had sneezing, nasal blockage and a runny nose every summer for years. This year symptoms wake her most nights and affect her work. She has not taken any treatment. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Examination shows swollen nasal turbinates with clear discharge.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis (interfering with sleep or work) is treated initially with an intranasal corticosteroid such as mometasone or fluticasone.

clues: wake her most nights and affect her work
steps.x: Symptoms affecting sleep and work: moderate to severe.

elim: Prolonged decongestant use causes rhinitis medicamentosa.
Oral steroids are reserved for severe cases, not first treatment.
Not initial management.
Combination sprays are for failure after 2 to 4 weeks; antibiotics have no role.

steps.x: A: Intranasal fluticasone. Moderate to severe allergic rhinitis: start an intranasal corticosteroid.

questions.stem: A 20 year old student with seasonal allergic rhinitis has found that an oxymetazoline nasal spray clears her blocked nose quickly. She plans to use it several times a day throughout her 2 month exam period. She already uses intranasal mometasone. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Examination shows swollen turbinates.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice about the oxymetazoline spray?
o: Double the dose if it stops working
Safe to use for the whole exam period
Stop the mometasone and use oxymetazoline instead
Use it daily for a year to prevent symptoms
Use it for a few days only
questions.e: Prolonged intranasal decongestant use leads to tachyphylaxis and rhinitis medicamentosa from rebound vasodilation, so it should be used only for a few days.

clues: several times a day throughout her 2 month exam period
steps.x: A topical decongestant planned for weeks.

elim: Worsens rebound congestion.
Prolonged use causes rhinitis medicamentosa.
The steroid is the right long-term treatment.
Long-term use causes tachyphylaxis and rebound.

steps.x: E: Use it for a few days only. Avoid prolonged decongestant sprays: rhinitis medicamentosa.

questions.stem: A 42 year old male mechanic has itchy eczematous dermatitis on the backs of both hands. Patch testing at 72 hours confirms allergy to a chemical in the rubber gloves he wears at work. The rash is moderately severe. His temperature is 36.6°C. There is no infection or weeping.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Allergic disorders are managed by avoiding the trigger, with steroids added if needed: topical for skin, nasal for rhinitis and oral only when severe.

clues: confirms allergy to a chemical in the rubber gloves
steps.x: A confirmed contact allergen and an inflamed skin rash.

elim: For anaphylaxis only.
Oral steroids are for severe cases and short courses only.
No sign of infection.
This is allergic dermatitis, not a fungal infection.

steps.x: E: Topical corticosteroid and glove avoidance. Avoid the trigger; steroid route matches the site: topical for skin.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl with known cow's milk allergy accidentally drinks a milkshake at a party. Ten minutes later she has widespread hives, lip swelling and wheeze, and feels dizzy. Her pulse rate is 146 bpm, BP 76/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. She has no auto-injector with her.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis, a complication of allergy, is treated first with IM adrenaline (300 micrograms at 6 to 12 years).

clues: widespread hives, lip swelling and wheeze
steps.x: Allergic reaction with breathing and circulation compromise.

elim: Antihistamines are supportive only and do not treat shock or airway swelling.
Not a first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.
Supportive for wheeze, but adrenaline comes first.
Too slow and does not treat ABC compromise.

steps.x: A: IM adrenaline. Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline first.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with anaphylaxis to a shellfish meal was given IM adrenaline 500 micrograms and high-flow oxygen 5 minutes ago. She still has stridor and wheeze. Her pulse rate is 138 bpm, BP 80/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 91% on 15 L/min oxygen. IV access is in place.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Repeat IM adrenaline with an IV fluid bolus
Wait 30 minutes for the first dose to work
questions.e: If there is no response to IM adrenaline, it is repeated after 5 minutes with an IV fluid bolus.

steps.x: No response 5 minutes after the first dose.

elim: Supportive only; does not treat ongoing shock.
Does not act quickly enough on airway or circulation.
Far too slow.
Adrenaline is repeated after 5 minutes if there is no response.

steps.x: D: Repeat IM adrenaline with an IV fluid bolus. No response at 5 minutes: repeat IM adrenaline and give IV fluid.

questions.stem: A 2 month old exclusively breastfed boy has cow's milk protein allergy with eczema and loose stools. His mother has removed all dairy from her diet and his symptoms have settled. She plans to continue breastfeeding for a year. Her BMI is 23 kg/m² and she takes no supplements. The baby is thriving.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management for the mother?
o: Stop breastfeeding and start soya formula
questions.e: Breastfeeding mothers excluding dairy should be considered for calcium (and vitamin D) supplements to protect their bone health.

clues: removed all dairy from her diet
steps.x: Long-term maternal dairy exclusion.

elim: Not specifically needed when excluding dairy.
Would cause his symptoms to return; reintroduction is planned later.
Breastfeeding should continue, and soya is not first choice.
Dairy exclusion alone does not cause B12 deficiency.

steps.x: B: Offer calcium supplements. Mother excluding dairy: consider calcium supplements.

questions.stem: A 13 month old girl with non-IgE-mediated cow's milk protein allergy has been well on an extensively hydrolysed formula since 4 months of age. She has had no symptoms for 6 months and is growing along the 50th centile. Her parents ask about trying cow's milk again. Examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Give a full glass of cow's milk in hospital
Reintroduce milk using the milk ladder
Skin prick test before any reintroduction
Switch to an amino acid formula
questions.e: In non-IgE cow's milk allergy, after about 6 months of symptom control (and from age 9 to 12 months), milk is reintroduced stepwise at home using the milk ladder.

steps.x: Well-controlled non-IgE allergy ready for reintroduction.

elim: Most children are tolerant by age 3, so reintroduction is attempted much earlier.
A stepwise ladder is used for non-IgE allergy, not a single large challenge.
Non-IgE allergy is not IgE-mediated, so the test does not guide reintroduction.
She is thriving on her current formula.

steps.x: C: Reintroduce milk using the milk ladder. Reintroduce cow's milk with the milk ladder.

questions.stem: A 7 month old boy has had eczema, reflux and diarrhoea since starting cow's milk formula at 3 months. His weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 2nd centile and he is irritable. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 130 bpm. He looks thin with widespread eczema. His GP suspects cow's milk protein allergy.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Suspected cow's milk protein allergy with faltering growth (failure to thrive) needs paediatric referral.

steps.x: Suspected milk allergy with faltering growth.

elim: Still contains cow's milk protein.
No role in suspected milk allergy.
Faltering growth needs prompt specialist input.
For reintroduction after a period of avoidance, not for an unwell infant.

steps.x: C: Paediatric referral. Cow's milk allergy plus failure to thrive: refer to paediatrics.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man was stung by a wasp last month. Within 15 minutes he had widespread hives, facial swelling and felt light-headed, settling with treatment in the emergency department. He works as a gardener. He has no other allergies. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Examination today is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Skin patch testing to wasp venom
questions.e: An insect sting causing a systemic reaction should prompt allergy specialist referral to confirm venom allergy and consider venom immunotherapy and adrenaline auto-injectors.

clues: widespread hives, facial swelling and felt light-headed
steps.x: A systemic reaction to a sting in someone with ongoing exposure.

elim: Does not prevent a severe systemic reaction.
A systemic reaction needs specialist assessment.
Patch tests are for delayed contact allergy.
No role.

steps.x: C: Referral to an allergy specialist. Systemic reaction to a sting: refer to an allergy specialist.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman had no reaction the first time she ate cashew nuts. Six months later she ate them again and developed urticaria and lip swelling within minutes. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm, BP 120/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. A student asks what happened at her first exposure.
questions.q: Which process most likely occurred at her first exposure?
o: Formation of IgG antibodies against red cells
Production of cashew-specific IgE that binds mast cells
Sensitisation of cytotoxic T cells in the skin
questions.e: In Type I hypersensitivity, first exposure produces allergen-specific IgE that binds Fc receptors on mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure the allergen cross-links IgE, triggering degranulation.

clues: ate them again and developed urticaria
steps.x: No reaction first time, rapid reaction second time.

elim: Type III hypersensitivity, as in serum sickness.
Type II hypersensitivity.
Happens on re-exposure, not at sensitisation.
Type IV delayed reaction.

steps.x: C: Production of cashew-specific IgE that binds mast cells. Type I: sensitisation makes IgE on mast cells; re-exposure cross-links it.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man develops raised, itchy wheals on his chest and swelling of his eyelids 10 minutes after eating prawns. His pulse rate is 94 bpm, BP 126/80 mmHg and oxygen saturation 99% breathing air. A student asks how histamine causes the raised wheals and swelling.
questions.q: Which effect of histamine most directly causes the wheals and swelling?
questions.e: Histamine causes vasodilation (redness) and increased vascular permeability, so fluid leaks into tissues causing wheals and angioedema; smooth muscle contraction causes bronchospasm.

steps.x: Fluid in the skin and soft tissues.

elim: Causes wheeze, not skin swelling.
Causes rhinorrhoea, not wheals.
Not a main effect of histamine.
Histamine causes vasodilation, not constriction.

steps.x: C: Increased vascular permeability. Wheals and angioedema = increased vascular permeability.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman develops an itchy, red, vesicular rash on her wrist 2 days after starting to wear a new metal watch. A patch test to nickel is positive when read at 72 hours, while a skin prick test to nickel is negative. Her temperature is 36.6°C. She has no urticaria elsewhere.
questions.q: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
questions.e: Allergic contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed T-cell-mediated reaction, which explains the 2 to 3 day delay and the negative skin prick test.

clues: 2 days after starting to wear a new metal watch
skin prick test to nickel is negative
steps.x: Delayed onset with a positive patch test and negative prick test.

elim: Immediate IgE-mediated wheal and flare within minutes.
Antibody against cell-surface antigens, as in haemolytic reactions.
Immune complex deposition, as in serum sickness.
A stimulating antibody, as in Graves' disease.

steps.x: D: Type IV. Contact dermatitis = Type IV, delayed, T-cell mediated.

questions.stem: A 5 month old girl has reflux, loose stools and eczema that settle on an extensively hydrolysed formula and return when cow's milk formula is restarted. Symptoms begin 1 to 2 days after milk. Skin prick testing and specific IgE to cow's milk are negative. She is thriving. Her parents ask why the allergy tests were negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the negative tests?
o: Testing was done too soon after birth
questions.e: Non-IgE-mediated food allergy is driven by T-cell mechanisms, explaining delayed onset, negative skin prick and RAST tests, and why elimination-reintroduction is used for diagnosis.

clues: Symptoms begin 1 to 2 days after milk
Skin prick testing and specific IgE to cow's milk are negative
return when cow's milk formula is restarted
steps.x: Delayed reaction, recurrence on reintroduction, negative IgE tests.

elim: Symptoms resolved on a hydrolysed protein formula and include eczema.
Would not affect specific IgE in blood.
Infants can make IgE; the timing is not the problem.
Symptoms recurred on reintroduction.

steps.x: C: T-cell-mediated rather than IgE-mediated reaction. Non-IgE allergy is T-cell mediated: IgE tests are negative.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has used xylometazoline nasal spray four times a day for 3 months. His nose is now constantly blocked and is only briefly relieved by the spray, so he uses it more often. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg. The nasal mucosa is red and swollen with no polyps.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his nasal blockage?
o: Squamous metaplasia of the nasal mucosa
questions.e: Prolonged topical alpha-agonist decongestant use causes receptor downregulation and rebound vasodilation (rhinitis medicamentosa), with tachyphylaxis driving ever more frequent use.

clues: xylometazoline nasal spray four times a day for 3 months
only briefly relieved by the spray
steps.x: Long-term decongestant use with diminishing relief.

elim: No allergen trigger is described; the pattern follows decongestant use.
No purulent discharge, fever or facial pain.
No polyps are seen.
Not the mechanism of rebound congestion.

steps.x: D: Rebound vasodilation from alpha-receptor downregulation. Rhinitis medicamentosa: alpha-receptor downregulation and rebound vasodilation.
